topic: China's share of equipment demand: SEMI/SEAJ regional billings vs equipment makers' China revenue shares
disagreement: SEMI/SEAJ billings put mainland China at 42.3% of world equipment billings in 2024 (US$49.55bn of US$117.14bn) and 36.5% in 2025 (US$49.31bn of US$135.06bn). Vendor disclosures give different China shares: Applied Materials 37% (FY2024) and 30% (FY2025, Nov-Oct); ASML 36.1% (2024) and 29.1% (2025); Tokyo Electron 42% (FY Apr 2024-Mar 2025); Lam 35% and KLA 30% (quarter to June 2025).
possible_reasons: period: SEMI is calendar year; AMAT fiscal year ends late October, TEL's ends March, Lam/KLA figures are single quarters

population: vendor revenue includes service, spares and upgrades (ASML installed-base management, AMAT Applied Global Services, AMAT also includes display equipment) while WWSEMS counts equipment billings
product mix: each vendor's share reflects its own tool mix; China bought relatively more mature-node etch/deposition and DUV than leading-edge EUV (which ASML cannot ship to China)
region assignment: ASML attributes sales to customer facility location; WWSEMS region rule is not defined in the release; vendors may book sales to China-located multinational fabs differently
coverage: WWSEMS includes Chinese domestic toolmakers (e.g. Naura, AMEC) that report to SEMI/SEAJ, whose sales are almost all in China; US/European/Japanese vendors' China shares exclude them
rationale: Not a true conflict: every figure is a primary disclosure (association statistic or company filing) but they measure different populations over different periods. All series agree on the direction: China's share peaked in 2024 and fell in 2025 (SEMI 42.3% to 36.5%; AMAT 37% to 30%; ASML 36.1% to 29.1%). Our arithmetic: 49.31/135.06 = 36.5%; 49.55/117.14 = 42.3%.
remaining_uncertainty: WWSEMS does not publish its regional assignment rule or the share of Chinese domestic vendors in China billings, so the gap between SEMI's China share and Western vendors' China shares cannot be decomposed.

topic: Semiconductor test equipment market size: SEMI test segment vs Advantest's tester (ATE) market
disagreement: SEMI's figures imply 2025 test equipment sales of about US$11.7bn (US$15.3bn 2026 forecast / 1.31; December 2025 forecast US$11.2bn), while Advantest sizes the 2025 tester market at about US$9.0bn (US$6.0bn in 2024 vs about US$7.5bn implied by SEMI for 2024).
possible_reasons: population: Advantest counts SoC and memory automatic test equipment only (excludes handlers, probers and interface boards); SEMI's test segment covers all semiconductor test equipment
methodology: SEMI aggregates member billings and forecasts (OEM perspective); Advantest's market estimate is internal and undisclosed
vintage: SEMI's 2025 value here is derived (our arithmetic: 15.3/1.31 = 11.68; 11.68/1.553 = 7.52 for 2024), not a stated actual
rationale: Different populations: the tester (ATE) market is a subset of SEMI's test segment. Advantest's figure is about 77% of the SEMI-implied 2025 test total (9.0/11.68) and about 80% in 2024 (6.0/7.52), a stable ratio consistent with ATE being most but not all of test equipment.
remaining_uncertainty: Neither source publishes the split of non-ATE test equipment (probers, handlers), so the residual cannot be verified.

topic: Price of one High-NA EUV (EXE) system
disagreement: Reuters (via TrendForce, Mar 2026) says an EXE:5200 costs roughly US$400m; CNBC (May 2025) 'more than US$400 million'; Korea Economic Daily reports Samsung paying KRW 1.1tn (US$773m) for two EXE:5200B, about US$386m each; ASML's 2025 revenue for 4 EXE systems was EUR 1,156.9m, an average of EUR 289m per system (EUR 232.5m per system for the 2 recognised in 2024).
possible_reasons: population: list/contract price of a new EXE:5200B vs average revenue recognised per EXE system in a year, which mixes EXE:5000 R&D tools and EXE:5200B and may exclude options recognised separately
currency and exchange rate: EUR vs USD vs KRW converted at an unstated rate
period: 2024-2026 statements; the EXE:5200B is a newer, more productive model than the EXE:5000
rounding: press 'roughly' and 'more than' figures
rationale: The three press figures agree (about US$386-400m+ per EXE:5200-class tool). ASML's audited average (EUR 289m, about US$310-330m at USD/EUR 1.08-1.13, our arithmetic) is lower because it is an average of recognised revenue across models and cannot be read as a price. No single figure is more defensible: ASML does not publish list prices.
remaining_uncertainty: Exact EXE:5200B transaction prices and what the reported amounts include (installation, options, service) are not public.

topic: Total semiconductor lithography market in units (2025): Nikon's market estimate vs sum of vendor unit sales
disagreement: Nikon estimates the 2025 semiconductor lithography market at about 570 units (new and refurbished, all vendors), but ASML (327 lithography systems, CY2025), Canon (234, CY2025) and Nikon itself (27, FY Apr 2025-Mar 2026) already add up to 588 units, about 3% more, before counting Chinese vendors such as SMEE.
possible_reasons: period: Nikon's own units are fiscal-year (April-March) while its market estimate is calendar-year
population: Canon's 234 units may include back-end (packaging) i-line steppers that Nikon's 'semiconductor lithography' market definition may exclude; Nikon does not state its definition
population: ASML's 327 includes used systems; Nikon's market counts new and refurbished, possibly treating used resales differently
methodology: Nikon's market size is an internal estimate with no disclosed method
rationale: The vendor figures are company-reported counts for their own sales and are more reliable than a competitor's market estimate, but the gap (588 vs 570, our arithmetic) is small and best explained by period and definition differences, so neither is wrong.
remaining_uncertainty: Chinese vendor unit shipments are not public, and Nikon does not disclose what its market estimate includes.

topic: TSMC CoWoS capacity expected at end-2027
disagreement: For end-2027 TSMC CoWoS capacity, TechNews-cited investors (Apr 2026) expect about 170,000 wafers/month, UBS (Sep 2026) about 180,000, and Commercial Times-cited investors (Aug 2026) 220,000: a 29% spread for the same company and date.
possible_reasons: methodology: unnamed sell-side models, none disclosed; TSMC publishes no capacity figure (CLM-0799)
population: whether outsourced chip-on-wafer or on-substrate steps done by OSATs for TSMC are counted, and whether CoWoS-S/-L/-R are converted to a common wafer basis, is not stated
vintage: April vs August vs September 2026; estimates have risen with each AI-capex revision
rationale: A true conflict between estimates of the same quantity. None can be preferred: all are tier-2/3 relays of anonymous or paywalled sell-side models with no stated basis. UBS's figure is internally consistent with its own industry total (270k = TSMC 180k + ASE 70k + Amkor ~20k) and is the most recent, but the 220k estimate may count capacity TSMC outsources to partners.
remaining_uncertainty: Unknowable from public data until TSMC discloses capacity; actual end-2027 capacity could fall anywhere in or outside the 170-220k range.

topic: Global semiconductor materials market size in SIA/BCG (2024) vs SEMI series
disagreement: SIA/BCG's 2024 report describes a US$64bn materials market (front-end US$40bn, back-end US$24bn), recorded as 'c. 2022'. SEMI put 2022 materials at US$72.7bn (fab US$44.7bn, packaging US$28.0bn). SEMI's first-reported 2021 figures are US$64.3bn, with fab US$40.4bn and packaging US$23.9bn, which match SIA/BCG's split.
possible_reasons: period: SIA/BCG's US$64bn matches SEMI's 2021 data (40.4 + 23.9 = 64.3), not 2022
vintage: SEMI later restated 2021 to US$66.8bn (CLM-1798); SIA/BCG used the first-reported vintage
rationale: The figures do not conflict once the year is fixed: the SIA/BCG number is SEMI's first-reported 2021 materials market. CLM-1810's period label 'c. 2022' should read 'probably 2021 (SEMI first-reported data)'. For the size of the materials market in any given year, use SEMI's series and its latest restatement.
remaining_uncertainty: SIA/BCG does not state the year of its materials figure; the match to SEMI 2021 is an inference from three numbers lining up.

topic: SEMI 2023 global semiconductor materials revenue: first report vs restatement
disagreement: SEMI first reported 2023 materials revenue as US$66.7bn (May 2024); its April 2025 release restated 2023 to US$64,994m (about US$65.0bn), 2.6% lower.
possible_reasons: vintage: SEMI revises prior-year data when member data and the MMDS model are updated (the same happened for 2020 and 2021, CON-0059/CON-0060)
rationale: Same publisher, same measure, same year: the later restatement is SEMI's current figure (as in CON-0059 and CON-0060).
remaining_uncertainty: SEMI does not explain the size of the revision; further restatements are possible.

topic: Size of a leading-edge fab: capex and TCO figures across sources
disagreement: Cost figures for 'one fab' range from US$7-20bn (CRS, c.2020), about US$20bn capex for a 5nm reference fab (SIA/BCG 2020), US$35-43bn 10-year TCO for a 2nm fab (BCG 2023), more than US$65bn for three TSMC Arizona fabs (about US$21.7bn each, our arithmetic), about KRW 50tn (US$36bn) for Samsung's Pyeongtaek P4 building, to KRW 31tn (about US$21.5bn) for SK hynix's first Yongin fab.
possible_reasons: population: capex only (building plus tools) vs 10-year total cost of ownership including operating costs
unit of a 'fab': a single cleanroom module vs a multi-cleanroom building (P4 has four cleanrooms; Yongin fab 1 has six) vs a multi-phase site
node and product: 5nm vs 2nm logic, memory, analog
period and inflation: 2020 vs 2023-2026 estimates; BCG says US construction costs rose 6% a year after 2021
scope: announced investment plans often include later phases, infrastructure and land, and are not audited spend
rationale: Not a conflict: the figures count different things. A beginner should read 'a leading-edge fab costs US$20bn+' as capex for one large module at 2020 prices; 2nm modules and multi-cleanroom memory buildings cost more, and 10-year TCO is about double capex.
remaining_uncertainty: No source gives audited per-fab capex for a recent leading-edge fab; company announcements bundle phases.

topic: TSMC advanced-packaging facility count: annual report (7 Advanced Backend Fabs) vs packaging VP (10 facilities)
disagreement: TSMC's 2025 annual report lists seven Advanced Backend Fabs, all in Taiwan; TSMC's VP of advanced packaging said in August 2026 that TSMC operates 10 advanced packaging facilities.
possible_reasons: period: annual report (published early 2026, status around end-2025) vs August 2026 statement; new AP facilities (e.g. Chiayi AP7 phases) opened in between
definition: 'facility' may count phases or buildings within one AP site separately, while the annual report lists sites
geography: the 10 may include facilities outside Taiwan or partner sites
rationale: Both are TSMC statements; the difference is most likely timing and counting unit, not an error. Use the annual report list for site names and the VP statement for the 2026 operating count.
remaining_uncertainty: TSMC does not publish a list of the 10 facilities.

topic: 2025 EDA and IP market size: Synopsys estimate vs ESD Alliance industry revenue
disagreement: Synopsys sizes the 2025 EDA and IP market at US$22.5bn; the sum of ESD Alliance quarterly revenue for 2025 is about US$21.2bn, 5.7% lower.
possible_reasons: population: ESD Alliance counts revenue reported by its EDMD participating companies (EDA, IP and services) and excludes non-reporting firms (notably many Chinese EDA vendors); Synopsys's scope is not disclosed
methodology: one is a company's market estimate on an investor slide, the other an aggregation of member-reported revenue
vintage: ESD Alliance Q1 2025 was restated
rationale: The two figures are broadly consistent and differ mainly in coverage; neither is wrong.
remaining_uncertainty: Synopsys's definition is not public, so the gap cannot be allocated.

topic: Size of the foundry market in 2025
disagreement: Synopsys sizes the 2025 foundry market at US$174.2bn; TrendForce's top-10 foundry revenue was about US$46.3bn in 4Q25 alone (about US$185bn annualised); TSMC's own 2025 revenue was US$122.42bn, 70% of the Synopsys figure; TSMC's 'Foundry 2.0' industry (logic wafer manufacturing incl. IDMs, packaging, test, masks) is far larger (about US$250bn already in 2023).
possible_reasons: population: pure-play foundry services vs top-10 foundries including Samsung Foundry vs Foundry 2.0 that adds IDM logic manufacturing and back-end
period: annual vs one quarter (annualising Q4 overstates the year in a rising market)
methodology: Synopsys does not disclose its source
rationale: Different definitions; see also CON-0004. A share of 'the foundry market' is only meaningful with the definition named: TSMC is about 70% of conventional foundry but only about 28% (2023) of Foundry 2.0.
remaining_uncertainty: Synopsys's foundry definition and source are not public.

topic: World semiconductor market forecast for 2026 across publishers and vintages
disagreement: 2026 forecasts range from US$1,320bn (Gartner, April 2026) through US$1,510bn (WSTS, June 2026) and about US$1,555bn (Gartner, August 2026: memory 837.3 + non-memory 717.9) to US$1,655bn (WSTS calculation after actual Q2 data, July 2026).
possible_reasons: vintage: forecasts made April-August 2026 during a memory price spike; each later forecast is higher

population: WSTS counts member-reported product sales (WSTS classification); Gartner models vendor revenue (2025 base US$809.0bn vs WSTS US$795.6bn) with a different memory/non-memory split (Gartner 2025 memory 220.1 vs WSTS 230.0; non-memory 589.0 vs 565.6, our arithmetic)
methodology: WSTS's US$1,655bn is not a full forecast round but the Spring forecast updated with actual Q2 data
rationale: Forecasts by different publishers on different populations; no figure is 'right' until 2026 actuals. Within each publisher the latest vintage supersedes earlier ones (WSTS: CON-0021; Gartner: April superseded by August). Both latest vintages imply roughly a doubling of the market in 2026.
remaining_uncertainty: Memory pricing in H2 2026 dominates the outcome; Gartner and WSTS do not reconcile their populations.

topic: TSMC 2026 capital budget guidance: January vs July 2026
disagreement: TSMC guided 2026 capex of US$52-56bn (January 2026) and US$60-64bn (July 2026).
possible_reasons: vintage: guidance raised in July 2026
rationale: Same company, same measure: the later guidance supersedes the earlier one.
remaining_uncertainty: Actual 2026 capex will only be known from TSMC's 2026 results.

topic: HBM thermo-compression bonder market size: ASMPT TCB addressable market vs TechInsights HBM TC-bonder revenue
disagreement: ASMPT estimates the TCB addressable market at about US$760m in 2025; TechInsights' figures (via Hanmi: Hanmi US$247.7m = 71.2% of HBM TC-bonder revenue through Q3 2025) imply an HBM TC-bonder market of about US$348m for the first nine months of 2025 (our arithmetic).
possible_reasons: population: HBM-only TC bonders vs all thermo-compression bonding including logic/advanced-packaging applications
period: Q1-Q3 2025 cumulative vs full year 2025
methodology: ASMPT's addressable-market model vs TechInsights' vendor revenue tracking
rationale: Different scopes and periods; annualising the HBM-only figure (about US$460m) still leaves logic/other TCB to explain the remainder. Not a conflict.
remaining_uncertainty: Neither source publishes a split of TCB demand by application.

topic: Status of the BIS affiliates-rule suspension after the US-China truce extension
disagreement: The Federal Register rule suspends the BIS affiliates (50%) rule only through 9 November 2026, after which it applies again unless further action is taken; on 24 September 2026 the US Treasury Secretary said the Busan truce would be extended to 10 January 2027, which law-firm commentary reads as pushing back the affiliates rule's return, but as of 30 September 2026 BIS had published no Federal Register notice extending the suspension.
possible_reasons: legal vs political status: a ministerial statement announces intent; the suspension end date only changes with a Federal Register notice
date wording: the suspension runs through 9 November (rule) and the rule applies again from 10 November; commentary describes the return as 'November 9'
rationale: As of 1 October 2026 the legal text (tier 1) still controls: the suspension ends after 9 November 2026. The truce extension is a credible announced intent (Bessent quote, CLM-2257) but is not yet law; treat 10 January 2027 as expected, not in force.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether and when BIS publishes an extension notice, and whether China extends its own parallel suspensions (MOFCOM Announcements 2025 No. 70 and No. 72, ending 10 and 27 November 2026), is unresolved.

topic: TSMC's share of 'the foundry market' in Q2 2026 across trackers and definitions
disagreement: For the same quarter (Q2 2026) and the same TSMC revenue (about US$40.2bn), TrendForce gives TSMC 72.5% of the foundry market and Counterpoint 73% of the pure-play foundry market, but Counterpoint gives only 42% of its 'Foundry 2.0' market; TSMC itself put its Foundry 2.0 share at 28% in 2023.
possible_reasons: population: TrendForce's denominator is a foundry total of about US$55.45bn (40.2/0.725, our arithmetic), larger than its US$53.49bn top-10 sum; Counterpoint's pure-play total is US$54.9bn (40.2/54.9 = 73.2%)
population: Foundry 2.0 adds non-memory IDM manufacturing, OSATs and photomask makers (Counterpoint: US$96.6bn in Q2 2026; TSMC's own definition about US$250bn for 2023)
period: TSMC's 28% is for 2023, before its AI-driven share gains
rationale: Not a conflict: the two conventional trackers agree (72.5% vs 73%). The share falls to 42% or 28% only because the Foundry 2.0 denominator is roughly 1.8x (Counterpoint) or more (TSMC) larger. A beginner should always ask which 'foundry market' a share refers to.
remaining_uncertainty: Neither tracker publishes its full company list or treatment of Samsung's internal foundry revenue; the Counterpoint Foundry 2.0 figures were read through a press relay.

topic: Silicon wafer market revenue in 2025: SEMI SMG reported vs TECHCET forecast
disagreement: SEMI's Silicon Manufacturers Group reported 2025 silicon wafer revenue down 1.2% to US$11.4bn; TECHCET had forecast revenue up 6.7% to US$13.6bn. Shipments agree closely (SEMI 12,973 MSI, +5.8%; TECHCET forecast 13,076 MSI, +5.4%).
possible_reasons: population: TECHCET's market includes SOI and possibly other wafer types; its implied 2024 base is about US$12.75bn (13.6/1.067) vs SEMI's about US$11.54bn (11.4/0.988), our arithmetic, a 10% different starting point
vintage: TECHCET's figure is a 2025 forecast; SEMI's is the year-end actual, in which revenue fell because legacy (200mm and smaller) pricing stayed weak
methodology: SEMI aggregates data from member wafer makers (semiconductor applications only); TECHCET models the market
rationale: Volumes agree, so the difference is scope plus a forecast miss on price. For 2025 actuals use SEMI SMG (tier 1, reported data). TECHCET is useful for its segment detail but its revenue figure is a forecast on a wider base.
remaining_uncertainty: TECHCET's actual 2025 outcome and exact scope are in a paywalled report.

topic: How much of DRAM is HBM: share of value vs share of wafers vs share of bits
disagreement: For 2025, Gartner puts HBM at 23% of DRAM market value; TrendForce at about 18% of the top three makers' DRAM wafer input (end-2025) but only about 8% of DRAM bit supply; Shin-Etsu at just under 20% of 300mm DRAM wafers; TrendForce had projected in 2024 that HBM could exceed 30% of DRAM value in 2025.
possible_reasons: unit: revenue share vs wafer share vs bit share; HBM dies are larger and stacked, so each wafer yields fewer bits but sells for more
population: top-three suppliers' wafer input (TrendForce) vs all 300mm DRAM wafers (Shin-Etsu) vs DRAM revenue (Gartner)
vintage: TrendForce's 30% value figure was a May 2024 projection
rationale: The wafer-based figures agree (18% vs just under 20%). The value share (23%) sits above the wafer share and far above the bit share (8%), which is what you expect for a premium product. These are different measures, not a conflict.
remaining_uncertainty: No public post-year TrendForce figure for HBM's 2025 share of DRAM revenue was found.

topic: Chip design share of semiconductor value added: SIA/BCG 2019 data (2021 report) vs 2022 data (2024 report)
disagreement: SIA/BCG's 2021 report gives chip design about 50% of 2019 industry value added; its 2024 report's Exhibit 2 (2022 data) splits design into logic 30%, DAO 17% and memory 9%, about 56% in total. Equipment is 11% (2019) vs 12% (2022); ATP 6% and materials 5% in both.
possible_reasons: period: 2019 vs 2022 (2022 was a peak year for logic and still-strong memory)
methodology: the 2024 exhibit splits design by product and measures wafer fabrication and ATP by installed capacity at facility location; the 2021 exhibit used a six-activity breakdown
rounding: 2022 shares as charted sum to 101%
rationale: Different years and slightly different breakdowns; both are SIA/BCG estimates. Use 'about half to just over half of value added comes from design' rather than a single number, and cite the year.
remaining_uncertainty: The 2022 split was read from chart text in the PDF; BCG's model is not public.
